title: Entanglement Swapping Scheduling for Quantum Repeater Chains under Decoherence during Classical Communications
authors: Jorge Benito Díaz, Andrés Agustí, Jabier Faba, Laura Ortiz, Luis Robledo, Vicente Martín
abstract: First-generation quantum repeaters are essential in distributing entanglement over long distances since they could mitigate losses in optical fiber. Repeaters split the total distance into shorter, easier to generate links. Then, entanglement swapping establishes long range entanglement by performing local measurements at the repeaters and heralding their results. In this work, we develop an analytical model that estimates the impact of decoherence during heralding for a given protocol. Furthermore, we identify a competition between two phenomena: as repeater count increases, so does entanglement generation, but the additive impact of memory decoherence on final entanglement rate increases too. Therefore, we find that an optimal number of repeaters exists. These findings could lead the design of future quantum networks, both in the inter-repeater distance and swapping timings.
summary: This paper provides an analytical model to optimize quantum repeater chains for long-distance entanglement distribution by accounting for memory decoherence. It compares three scheduling strategies—Parallel, Tree, and Hybrid—to determine the entanglement rate as a function of repeater count. The key finding is that an optimal number of repeaters exists, balancing the benefits of shorter links against the cumulative decoherence penalty.
main_problem: The paper develops an analytical model to estimate the impact of decoherence during the heralding process in quantum repeaters used for long-distance entanglement distribution.
main_result: The analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off: while increasing the number of repeaters boosts entanglement generation, the additive penalty from memory decoherence eventually dominates, proving the existence of an optimal repeater count.
method: The authors developed an analytical framework comparing three scheduling strategies (Binary-Tree, Parallel, Hybrid) to calculate the entanglement rate by accounting for memory exposure during entanglement generation and swapping.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a homogeneous linear chain of N quantum repeaters connecting two end nodes over a total distance L_tot. The process involves sequential entanglement generation (EG) followed by entanglement swapping (ES) operations.
key_observables: Entanglement rate (measured using logarithmic negativity) and the optimal number of repeaters (N).
important_parameters: Memory decoherence time ($\tau$), total distance ($L_{tot}$), and the number of repeaters ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to prepare-and-swap strategies, and it models memory decoherence as an exponential time-decay of the Werner parameter.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the entanglement rate vs. N for a metropolitan scenario across different $\tau$; Figure 2 shows the rate vs. N for an intermetropolitan scenario, demonstrating an optimal N exists.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the need for an analytical framework. It then details the comparison of three scheduling strategies (Parallel, Tree, Hybrid) by quantifying memory exposure during the two main phases (generation and swapping). Finally, it presents results showing the dependence of the optimal repeater count on the decoherence time and distance scale.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of scaling quantum networks by quantifying the detrimental effects of decoherence and classical communication delays on entanglement distribution protocols.
